title: Unit 2 Question Bank
source: U2 guided-notes keys (verified fact sheet, 2026-11-09); U2 study guide
directions: Choose the best answer for each question.

groups.title: The Geologic Time Scale
groups.target: I can describe how geologists build the geologic time scale and read Earth's history from fossils and rock layers.

items.stem: Which of these is a trace fossil?
items.why: Trace fossils record activity: tracks, trails, burrows, coprolites.

wrong.B: A tooth is a preserved body part: a body fossil.
wrong.C: Wood is a preserved part of the organism: a body fossil.
wrong.D: A shell is a preserved body part: a body fossil.

items.stem: Which of these is a body fossil?
items.why: Body fossils are preserved parts: bones, teeth, shells, wood, leaves.

wrong.A: A burrow records activity: a trace fossil.
wrong.C: Tracks record activity: a trace fossil.
wrong.D: Coprolites (fossil dung) are listed as trace fossils.

items.stem: Why are bones, teeth and shells fossilized more often than soft body parts?
options: Soft parts cannot be buried by sediment
They are durable, so they last long enough to be buried
Soft parts turn into rock too quickly
items.why: Durable tissues are more likely to survive.

wrong.A: Anything can be buried; soft parts rot first.
wrong.C: Lifespan is not the reason; durability is.
wrong.D: Soft parts usually decay before they fossilize.

items.stem: A trace fossil is useful because it shows...
options: what an organism did, even if its body is missing
the exact age of the rock layer
what the organism's bones looked like
items.why: Trace fossils record biological activity; the organism itself may be absent.

wrong.B: Ages come from radiometric dating.
wrong.C: That would be a body fossil.
wrong.D: Tracks and burrows do not preserve color.

items.stem: Minerals fill the tiny pores in a buried bone, and some of the original bone remains. This is called...
items.why: Permineralization: minerals fill pores; original material may remain.

wrong.A: In replacement, minerals take the place of the dissolving original.
wrong.B: Carbonization leaves a flattened carbon film.
wrong.D: A cast fills a hollow mold.

items.stem: Minerals take the place of a shell's original material as it slowly dissolves. This is called...
items.why: Replacement: minerals substitute for the original material as it dissolves.

wrong.A: Permineralization fills pores; the original can remain.
wrong.C: Carbonization flattens remains into a carbon film.
wrong.D: A trace fossil records activity, not a replaced body part.

items.stem: A thin black film shaped like a fern leaf is found in a layer of shale. This fossil formed by...
items.why: Burial flattens remains; a thin carbon film may preserve a leaf or fern.

wrong.A: Permineralization fills pores in 3-D material like wood or bone.
wrong.B: A cast is a 3-D filling of a mold, not a thin film.
wrong.C: Replacement swaps minerals for the original; it does not leave a carbon film.

items.stem: A shell is buried and later dissolves, leaving a hollow shell-shaped space in the rock. This space is a...
items.why: A mold is the hollow impression left after buried material dissolves or decays.

wrong.A: A cast is what fills the mold.
wrong.B: A mold preserves the shape of the body, not an activity.
wrong.C: A carbon film is a flattened layer, not a hollow space.

items.source: S2.1 How fossils form: mold vs. cast

items.stem: Sediment fills a mold and hardens into a 3-D copy of the shell. This copy is a...
options: body fossil of the original shell
items.why: A cast is sediment or minerals filling a mold, making a 3-D replica.

wrong.A: The mold is the hollow space; the filling is the cast.
wrong.B: The original shell dissolved; this is a replica.
wrong.C: A carbon film is flat, not a 3-D copy.

items.source: S2.1 How fossils form: mold vs. cast

items.stem: Petrified wood can show which fossil processes?
items.why: The notes: petrified wood can show both processes.

wrong.A: Carbonization makes a flat film, not petrified wood.
wrong.B: Petrified wood keeps the wood's structure in minerals.
wrong.C: Wood is part of the organism, so it is a body fossil.

items.stem: Most fossils are found in which kind of rock?
items.why: Most fossils occur in sedimentary rock (must-write line).

wrong.A: Igneous rock forms from melted rock, which destroys remains.
wrong.B: Heat and pressure usually destroy fossils.
wrong.C: Fossils are concentrated in sedimentary rock.

items.stem: Why are most fossils found in sedimentary rock?
options: Cooling lava seals the remains inside
Layers of sediment bury and preserve remains
Heat and pressure harden the remains
Sedimentary rock is the oldest rock
items.why: Layers of sediment bury and preserve remains (must-write line).

wrong.A: Lava forms igneous rock and burns remains.
wrong.C: That describes metamorphism, which destroys fossils.
wrong.D: Its age is not why it holds fossils.

items.stem: Radiometric dating finds a mineral's age by measuring...
options: a radioactive parent isotope and its decay products
how thick the rock layers are
how many fossils the rock contains
how deep the rock is buried
items.why: Definition from the notes.

wrong.B: Layer thickness does not give an age in years.
wrong.C: Fossil count does not give an age.
wrong.D: Depth alone does not give an age in years.

items.stem: What is a half-life?
options: The time it takes for half of the parent atoms to decay
Half of the rock's total age
The time it takes for all of the parent atoms to decay
The time it takes to form half of a rock layer
items.why: Definition from the notes.

wrong.B: A half-life is a decay rate, not half an age.
wrong.C: That would be the whole sample; a half-life is half.
wrong.D: Half-life describes atoms decaying, not layers forming.

items.stem: Which method is best for dating a rock that is 2 billion years old?
options: Measuring how thick the layer is
items.why: Uranium-lead and potassium-argon date very ancient rock.

wrong.B: Carbon-14 only works for material younger than about 50,000 years.
wrong.C: Fossil counts do not give an age in years.
wrong.D: Thickness does not give an age in years.

items.stem: Carbon-14 dating would work best for which object?
options: A dinosaur bone 70 million years old
A piece of wood 5,000 years old
items.why: Carbon-14 dates organic material younger than about 50,000 years.

wrong.A: Far too old for carbon-14: a common mix-up.
wrong.C: Very old rock is dated with uranium-lead.
wrong.D: Far too old; use uranium-lead or potassium-argon.

items.stem: Carbon-14 can date organic material that is younger than about...
items.why: Carbon-14 dates material younger than about 50,000 years.

wrong.A: Too short; the limit is about 50,000.
wrong.C: Far beyond carbon-14's range.
wrong.D: That is the age of Earth.

items.stem: Radiometric dating gives the age of a mineral. That age usually tells when...
options: the fossils in the layer died
items.why: A mineral's age usually records when it crystallized (must-write line).

wrong.A: Not necessarily the age of the whole layer around it.
wrong.C: The mineral's clock started when it crystallized.
wrong.D: Digging it up does not reset the clock.

items.stem: Which list puts the units of geologic time in order from largest to smallest?
items.why: The four units, largest to smallest.

wrong.A: The eon is larger than the era.
wrong.B: That is smallest to largest.
wrong.C: The era is larger than the period.

items.stem: Which is the smallest unit of geologic time?
items.why: Eon, era, period, epoch: the epoch is smallest.

wrong.B: Periods are divided into epochs.
wrong.C: Eras are divided into periods.
wrong.D: The eon is the largest unit.

items.stem: About how long ago did Earth form?
items.why: From the notes.

wrong.A: That is when the Cenozoic began.
wrong.B: That is when the Cambrian began.
wrong.C: Off by a factor of 1,000: billion, not million.

items.stem: About how long ago did the Cambrian Period begin?
items.why: From the notes.

wrong.A: That is the start of the Cenozoic.
wrong.B: That is the start of the Mesozoic.
wrong.D: That is when Earth formed.

items.stem: About how long ago did the Mesozoic Era begin?
items.why: From the notes; the end-Permian extinction ended the Paleozoic then.

wrong.A: That is when the Mesozoic ended and the Cenozoic began.
wrong.C: That is the start of the Cambrian.
wrong.D: That is the Great Oxidation Event.

items.stem: We live in the Holocene. Which era is that part of?
items.why: The Holocene is in the Quaternary, the latest period of the Cenozoic (began 66 million years ago).

wrong.A: The Mesozoic ended 66 million years ago.
wrong.B: The Paleozoic ended 252 million years ago.
wrong.C: The Precambrian ended 539 million years ago.

items.source: S2.1 Time scale: Cenozoic begins; S2.3 Quaternary

groups.title: Eons, Eras, Epochs & Periods
groups.target: I can describe the Precambrian's place in Earth's history and the major events of its three eons.

items.stem: About how much of Earth's history does the Precambrian cover?
items.why: An informal span covering about 88% of Earth's history.

wrong.A: That is the part that comes after the Precambrian.
wrong.B: Far more than half.
wrong.C: Too low; about 88%.

items.stem: Which statement about the Precambrian is true?
options: It is the most recent eon
It is an informal span, not a true eon
It is an era of the Paleozoic
It covers about 12% of Earth's history
items.why: The notes: an informal span (not a true eon).

wrong.A: It is the oldest stretch of time.
wrong.C: It comes before the Paleozoic.
wrong.D: It covers about 88%.

items.stem: Which list puts the three Precambrian eons in order from oldest to youngest?
items.why: From the notes.

wrong.A: The Hadean comes first.
wrong.B: That is youngest to oldest.
wrong.D: The Archean comes before the Proterozoic.

items.stem: What is the oldest eon?
items.why: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic.

wrong.B: The Archean is the middle eon.
wrong.C: The Proterozoic is the youngest Precambrian eon.
wrong.D: The Cambrian is a period, not an eon.

items.stem: In the Hadean, dense iron-rich metal sank toward Earth's center. What did it form?
items.why: Hadean: dense iron-rich metal sinks to form the core.

wrong.A: The crust is the light outer layer.
wrong.C: Oceans develop in the Archean.
wrong.D: The atmosphere is gas, not sinking metal.

items.stem: Long-lasting crust, oceans and microbial ecosystems first developed in which eon?
items.why: Archean: long-lived crust, oceans, and microbial ecosystems develop.

wrong.A: The Hadean is when Earth accretes and the core forms.
wrong.B: The Proterozoic is when oxygen rises.
wrong.C: The Paleozoic is an era that starts with the Cambrian, much later.

items.stem: What kind of life lived in the Archean?
items.why: Archean: microbial ecosystems develop.

wrong.A: Trilobites appear in the Cambrian Explosion.
wrong.B: Land plants appear in the Ordovician.
wrong.D: Jawless fishes flourish in the Ordovician.

items.stem: In which eon did atmospheric oxygen rise and eukaryotes, then multicellular life, diversify?
items.why: Proterozoic, from the notes.

wrong.A: The Hadean is Earth forming its core.
wrong.B: The Archean has microbial ecosystems, before oxygen rises.
wrong.C: The Cenozoic is an era, and much later.

items.stem: About when did the Great Oxidation Event begin?
items.why: Began about 2.4 billion years ago.

wrong.D: That is when Earth formed.
wrong.B: That is the start of the Cambrian.
wrong.A: That is the end-Permian extinction.

items.stem: What caused the Great Oxidation Event?
options: Volcanoes released large amounts of oxygen
Photosynthesis released oxygen faster than rocks and iron could absorb it
The oceans froze and gave off oxygen
items.why: Cause, from the notes.

wrong.A: The oxygen came from photosynthesis.
wrong.C: No impact is involved; that is the K–Pg story.
wrong.D: Ice does not release oxygen; photosynthesis did.

items.stem: Why was the Great Oxidation Event a turning point for life?
options: It caused the Cambrian Explosion right away
It made life move onto land
It made complex, oxygen-using life possible
items.why: Must-write: rising oxygen made complex, oxygen-using life possible.

wrong.A: The Cambrian began nearly 2 billion years later.
wrong.B: Life moved onto land in the Paleozoic.
wrong.C: It was toxic to many anaerobic microbes, not all life.

items.stem: Rising oxygen was toxic to which living things?
items.why: Must-write: rising oxygen was toxic to many anaerobic microbes.

wrong.A: Land plants appear much later.
wrong.B: Dinosaurs appear about 2 billion years later.
wrong.C: Oxygen made these possible.

items.stem: Snowball Earth was made up of which two glaciations?
items.why: The Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations.

wrong.A: Those are periods, not glaciations.
wrong.C: Those are eons.
wrong.D: Those are landmasses that collided in the Silurian.

items.stem: About when did Snowball Earth happen?
items.why: Roughly 720–635 million years ago.

wrong.A: That is the Pleistocene ice ages, much later.
wrong.B: That is the end-Permian extinction.
wrong.D: That is when Earth formed.

items.stem: Snowball Earth happened during which eon?
items.why: The notes place it under OXYGEN AND ICE IN THE PROTEROZOIC.

wrong.A: The Hadean is Earth forming.
wrong.C: Snowball Earth came later, about 720–635 million years ago.
wrong.D: The Paleozoic is an era, and it began 539 million years ago.

groups.title: Period-by-Period Deep Dive
groups.target: I can describe what life, the surface, and the climate looked like in each geologic period.

items.stem: What was the Cambrian Explosion?
options: The first appearance of life on Earth
A rapid diversification of animal body plans
items.why: The Cambrian Explosion rapidly diversifies animal body plans.

wrong.A: It was a burst of new life, not an eruption.
wrong.B: The impact story is the K–Pg extinction.
wrong.C: Microbes lived billions of years earlier.

items.stem: Where did all life live during the Cambrian?
options: On land and in the sea
items.why: Life is still entirely marine.

wrong.A: Land plants appear in the Ordovician.
wrong.C: Nothing lived on land yet.
wrong.D: Cambrian life was marine.

items.stem: Trilobites are common Cambrian fossils. What kind of animal were they?
items.why: Arthropods (trilobites) appear in the Cambrian Explosion.

wrong.A: Fish are chordates; trilobites are arthropods.
wrong.C: Reptiles appear in the Carboniferous.
wrong.D: Dinosaurs appear in the Triassic.

items.stem: How long did the Cambrian Explosion take?
items.why: Must-write: tens of millions of years, not overnight.

wrong.A: "Explosion" means fast for geology, not overnight.
wrong.C: Far too short.
wrong.D: Far too long.

items.stem: Why is the Burgess Shale important?
options: It preserves soft-bodied animals that ordinary fossilization loses
It is the oldest rock on Earth
It holds the first dinosaur eggs
It is where most coal formed
items.why: Must-write line.

wrong.B: It is Cambrian, about half a billion years old.
wrong.C: Dinosaurs come much later.
wrong.D: Coal formed in Carboniferous wetlands.

items.stem: What was the Cambrian climate like?
options: Greenhouse, with high sea levels and less oxygen than today
An ice age, with low sea levels
Cold and dry, with more oxygen than today
Hot, with deserts covering most land
items.why: Cambrian Climate, from the notes.

wrong.B: That describes the late Ordovician.
wrong.C: Oxygen was lower than today.
wrong.D: Shallow seas spread widely.

items.stem: Cambrian shallow seas left sand, mud and lime that became which rocks?
items.why: Cambrian Earth, from the notes.

wrong.A: Those are igneous rocks.
wrong.B: Those are metamorphic rocks.
wrong.C: Not the Cambrian sediments named in the notes.

items.stem: The ancient landmass Laurentia includes the core of which modern continent?
items.why: Laurentia includes the core of modern North America.

wrong.A: Africa was part of Gondwana.
wrong.C: Antarctica was part of Gondwana.
wrong.D: Europe's core was Baltica.

items.stem: What happened to the climate late in the Ordovician?
options: It warmed and sea level rose
It cooled, ice grew and sea level fell
It stayed warm with no ice
items.why: Ordovician Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: That is the Silurian recovery.
wrong.C: Ice grew late in the period.
wrong.D: That is the end-Permian story.

items.stem: What followed the late-Ordovician cooling?
items.why: Major extinctions follow the late-period cooling.

wrong.A: That came before the Ordovician.
wrong.B: Dinosaurs appear in the Triassic.
wrong.C: That is the Cretaceous.

items.stem: Which pair flourished in Ordovician seas?
items.why: Reefs and jawless fishes flourish.

wrong.B: Whales are Cenozoic mammals.
wrong.C: Those are Mesozoic reptiles.
wrong.D: Those diversify in the Devonian.

items.stem: In which period did early land plants first appear?
items.why: Ordovician Life: early land plants appear.

wrong.A: Cambrian life was entirely marine.
wrong.B: By then there were wetland forests.
wrong.C: Flowering plants spread then, long after the first land plants.

items.stem: Laurentia and Baltica came together in Caledonian mountain building during which period?
items.why: Silurian Earth, from the notes.

wrong.B: Shallow seas spread then; no Caledonian collision.
wrong.C: Pangaea was splitting apart then.
wrong.D: The Himalaya and Andes were growing then.

items.stem: Which group diversified in the Silurian?
items.why: Jawed fishes and eurypterids diversify.

wrong.A: Dinosaurs appear in the Triassic.
wrong.C: They spread in the Cretaceous.
wrong.D: They diversify in the Neogene.

items.stem: What did small vascular plants and land arthropods build in the Silurian?
options: The first land communities and soils
items.why: Silurian Life, from the notes.

wrong.B: Reefs flourished in the Ordovician, in the sea.
wrong.C: Coal comes from Carboniferous wetlands.
wrong.D: Grasslands spread in the Neogene.

items.stem: What happened to sea levels in the Silurian?
options: They recovered as Earth warmed after the Ordovician glaciation
They fell as ice sheets grew
They dropped to the lowest ever
They stayed frozen in Snowball Earth
items.why: Warming after the Ordovician glaciation helps sea levels recover.

wrong.B: That is the late Ordovician.
wrong.C: They were recovering.
wrong.D: Snowball Earth was in the Proterozoic.

items.stem: Forests, insects and early tetrapods spread across the land in which period?
items.why: Devonian Life, from the notes.

wrong.A: Cambrian life was entirely marine.
wrong.B: Only early land plants appeared then.
wrong.D: By then land life was rebuilding after the end-Permian.

items.stem: Placoderms, early cartilaginous fish and lobe-finned fish diversified in which period?
items.why: Devonian Life, from the notes (the "Age of Fishes").

wrong.B: Body plans diversified, but these fish came later.
wrong.C: Synapsids and sauropsids were the story then.
wrong.D: Mammals diversified then.

items.stem: How did the Devonian end?
options: With late-Devonian extinctions that hit hard
items.why: Late-Devonian extinctions hit hard.

wrong.A: That is the K–Pg extinction.
wrong.B: That is the end-Permian extinction.
wrong.D: That was in the Proterozoic.

items.stem: Where did reefs thrive in the Devonian?
items.why: Devonian Earth: reefs thrive in warm shallow seas.

wrong.B: The Devonian seas were warm.
wrong.C: Reefs need warm, shallow water.
wrong.D: Reefs are marine.

items.stem: Thick coal deposits come from which Carboniferous environment?
options: Tropical wetlands that buried thick plant material
items.why: Tropical wetlands bury thick organic deposits that later become coal.

wrong.A: Coal is buried plant material, not ash.
wrong.C: Dinosaurs come much later; coal is from plants.
wrong.D: Those leave salt, not coal.

items.stem: Meganeura and Arthropleura were...
items.why: Giant arthropods dominate wet habitats on land.

wrong.B: Dinosaurs appear in the Triassic.
wrong.C: These lived on land, not in the sea.
wrong.D: They are animals.

items.stem: Why was the amniotic egg a major step?
options: It let animals reproduce away from standing water
items.why: Must-write: the amniotic egg let vertebrates reproduce away from standing water.

wrong.A: It is about eggs, not breathing.
wrong.B: Dinosaurs come later; it is about reproduction.
wrong.C: It is an animal egg.

items.stem: What happened to atmospheric oxygen in the Carboniferous?
options: It stayed the same as today
It rose above modern levels as CO₂ declined
items.why: Carboniferous Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: It rose above modern levels.
wrong.B: It rose above today's levels.
wrong.D: CO₂ declined while oxygen rose.

items.stem: In the Carboniferous, the tropics stayed warm and humid while which region glaciated?
items.why: Carboniferous Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: Laurentia lay in the warm tropics.
wrong.B: The notes name southern Gondwana as the region that glaciated.
wrong.C: That basin opened in the Jurassic.

items.stem: In the Permian, the supercontinent Pangaea was surrounded by one ocean named...
items.why: Pangaea is surrounded by one ocean (Panthalassa).

wrong.A: The Atlantic opened in the Jurassic, when Pangaea split.
wrong.B: It opened in the Jurassic.
wrong.D: The Tethys was a sea along Pangaea's eastern margin, not the surrounding ocean.

items.stem: Dimetrodon looked like a reptile. What was it really?
options: A synapsid, on the mammal line
items.why: Must-write: a synapsid, not a dinosaur.

wrong.B: The most common mix-up; dinosaurs appear later, in the Triassic.
wrong.C: Pterosaurs are Mesozoic flying reptiles.
wrong.D: It lived on land.

items.stem: What were Permian interior regions far from the coast like?
items.why: Permian Earth, from the notes.

wrong.A: That describes Carboniferous tropical wetlands.
wrong.B: That is the Quaternary.
wrong.D: That is the Cambrian or Jurassic.

items.stem: What set up a crisis at the end of the Permian?
options: Too much oxygen in the oceans
Severe warming and widespread ocean oxygen loss
items.why: Permian Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: The end-Permian was warming, not cooling.
wrong.B: The oceans lost oxygen.
wrong.D: Grasslands spread in the Neogene.

items.stem: When did dinosaurs first appear?
options: In the Jurassic, about 150 million years ago
In the Permian, about 252 million years ago
In the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago
In the Triassic, about 230 million years ago
items.why: Must-write: dinosaurs first appear in the Triassic, roughly 230 million years ago.

wrong.A: That is Archaeopteryx.
wrong.B: That is the end-Permian extinction.
wrong.C: That is when non-bird dinosaurs died out.

items.stem: Were dinosaurs the dominant land animals when they first appeared?
options: No, they appeared in the Triassic but were not yet dominant
Yes, they ruled from the moment they appeared
No, because they lived only in the sea
Yes, because mammals had already died out
items.why: Must-write: not yet the dominant land animals.

wrong.B: They were not yet dominant in the Triassic.
wrong.C: Dinosaurs lived on land.
wrong.D: Mammals were present and survived.

items.stem: What happened to ecosystems early in the Triassic?
options: They were destroyed by an asteroid
They moved onto land for the first time
They rebuilt after the end-Permian crisis
items.why: Triassic Life, from the notes.

wrong.A: That is the K–Pg, at the end of the Cretaceous.
wrong.B: That was in the Proterozoic.
wrong.C: Life reached land in the Paleozoic.

items.stem: Late in the Triassic, what began to happen to Pangaea?
items.why: Late-Triassic rifting begins the breakup.

wrong.B: It assembled in the Carboniferous and Permian.
wrong.C: Triassic interiors were hot and dry.
wrong.D: Rodinia was a Proterozoic supercontinent.

items.stem: What were Triassic interior regions like?
items.why: Triassic Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: Glaciers belong to the late Ordovician or Quaternary.
wrong.B: That is the Carboniferous.
wrong.D: That is the Cretaceous.

items.stem: Which new ocean basins opened in the Jurassic as Pangaea split apart?
options: The Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico
items.why: Jurassic Earth, from the notes.

wrong.A: Those already surrounded and bordered Pangaea.
wrong.B: Those are supercontinents, not oceans.
wrong.C: Those are landmasses, not oceans.

items.stem: Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus were...
items.why: Jurassic Life, from the notes.

wrong.A: Allosaurus is the Jurassic theropod named.
wrong.B: Those are pterosaurs.
wrong.D: Those are ichthyosaurs.

items.stem: Pterosaurs were...
items.why: Pterosaurs: flying reptiles, not dinosaurs (must-write).

wrong.A: A common mix-up: pterosaurs are reptiles but not dinosaurs.
wrong.B: Archaeopteryx is the bird-origin dinosaur.
wrong.D: Giant insects like Meganeura are Carboniferous arthropods.

items.stem: Ichthyosaurs were...
items.why: Must-write: ichthyosaurs are reptiles, not dinosaurs.

wrong.A: They are reptiles but not dinosaurs.
wrong.C: They are reptiles.
wrong.D: Whales are Cenozoic mammals.

items.stem: Why is Archaeopteryx important?
options: It is a feathered dinosaur near the origin of birds
items.why: About 150 million years ago, near the origin of birds.

wrong.A: Dinosaurs appear about 230 million years ago.
wrong.B: Pterosaurs are not dinosaurs; Archaeopteryx is.
wrong.D: It lived about 150 million years ago, long before.

items.stem: What was the Jurassic climate like?
options: Ice age, with low sea levels
Greenhouse, with shallow seas covering large areas
items.why: Jurassic Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: That describes the late Ordovician.
wrong.B: That is the Neogene.
wrong.D: That is the Proterozoic.

items.stem: Flowering plants (angiosperms) spread and diversified in which period?
items.why: Cretaceous Life, from the notes.

wrong.A: Only early land plants appeared then.
wrong.B: Wetland plants made coal, but flowering plants came later.
wrong.D: Grasslands spread then, after flowering plants.

items.stem: In the Cretaceous, what grew even in Antarctica during warm intervals?
items.why: Even Antarctica supports forests during warm intervals.

wrong.A: That is the Quaternary.
wrong.C: Reefs are marine.
wrong.D: That is the Neogene.

items.stem: What were Cretaceous sea levels like?
options: Low, because of huge ice sheets
High, flooding broad areas of the continents
items.why: Cretaceous Earth and Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: The Cretaceous was a greenhouse.
wrong.B: The seas were warm.
wrong.C: They were much higher.

items.stem: Were mammals alive during the Cretaceous?
options: No, mammals appeared only after the dinosaurs died
Yes, and they were the largest land animals
No, mammals appeared first in the Quaternary
items.why: Mammals were already present, though small.

wrong.A: A common mix-up: mammals lived alongside dinosaurs.
wrong.B: Dinosaurs were the largest; mammals were small.
wrong.D: Mammals were present in the Cretaceous.

items.stem: Fossil tracks and eggs mostly tell paleontologists about a dinosaur's...
items.why: Must-write: tracks and eggs for behavior.

wrong.A: Skulls and bones show identity.
wrong.B: Dated rock layers show when it lived.
wrong.C: Tracks and eggs do not show color.

items.stem: How do paleontologists know when a dinosaur lived and died out?
options: From the shape of its skull
From carbon-14 dating of its bones
items.why: Must-write: dated rock layers for when they lived and died out.

wrong.A: Skulls and bones show identity.
wrong.B: Tracks show behavior.
wrong.D: Dinosaur bones are far too old for carbon-14.

items.stem: Mammals diversified rapidly into the space left after the K–Pg extinction in which period?
items.why: Paleogene Life, from the notes.

wrong.A: The K–Pg extinction ended the Cretaceous.
wrong.B: That followed the end-Permian, not the K–Pg.
wrong.D: Jawed fishes diversified then.

items.stem: India colliding with Asia began building which mountain belt?
items.why: Paleogene Earth, from the notes.

wrong.A: The Appalachians grew in the Carboniferous.
wrong.C: Those formed when Laurentia and Baltica met in the Silurian.
wrong.D: The Andes are part of the Circum-Pacific belt.

items.stem: What did the climate do in the Paleogene?
options: It warmed into a new greenhouse
It cooled gradually as the Mesozoic greenhouse faded
It stayed the same as the Cretaceous
items.why: Paleogene Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: It cooled.
wrong.C: That was in the Proterozoic.
wrong.D: It cooled gradually.

items.stem: Grasslands spread widely and grazing mammals diversified in which period?
items.why: Neogene Life, from the notes.

wrong.A: Flowering plants spread then, before grasslands.
wrong.C: That was the age of coal swamps.
wrong.D: Forests first spread then.

items.stem: What did global climate do in the Neogene?
options: It became a greenhouse with high seas
It cooled further and dried in many regions
items.why: Neogene Climate, from the notes.

wrong.A: It cooled and dried.
wrong.B: That describes the Cretaceous.
wrong.C: That was in the Proterozoic.

items.stem: Continental ice sheets several kilometers thick advanced and retreated in which period?
items.why: Quaternary Earth, from the notes.

wrong.A: The Cambrian was a greenhouse.
wrong.B: The Jurassic was a greenhouse.
wrong.D: Cooling began then, but the ice sheets came in the Quaternary.

items.stem: What paces the Quaternary's glacial cycles?
items.why: Paced by Milankovitch orbital cycles.

wrong.A: Volcanoes are not what the notes name.
wrong.B: Impacts are not regular cycles.
wrong.D: Plate motion is far too slow to pace these cycles.

items.stem: What is the Holocene?
items.why: Must-write: we now live in the Holocene, the current interglacial.

wrong.A: It is the warm interglacial between glacial times.
wrong.B: Dinosaurs lived in the Mesozoic.
wrong.C: The Pleistocene ended 11,700 years ago.

items.stem: The Pleistocene ran from...
options: 2.58 million years ago to 11,700 years ago
items.why: Must-write line.

wrong.A: That is the Mesozoic Era.
wrong.B: That is Snowball Earth.
wrong.D: That is the Holocene.

items.stem: Human evolution happened during which period's repeated glacial cycles?
items.why: Human evolution occurs during the Quaternary's repeated glacial cycles.

wrong.B: Humans evolved long after the dinosaurs.
wrong.C: Mammals diversified then, but humans came later.
wrong.D: Far too early; the Permian is Paleozoic.

groups.title: Supercontinents Through Time
groups.target: I can trace how supercontinents assembled and broke apart across Earth's history.

items.stem: Which supercontinent formed first?
items.why: Rodinia assembled roughly 1.1–0.9 billion years ago; Pangaea in the Permian.

wrong.A: Pangaea assembled in the Permian, much later.
wrong.B: Panthalassa is an ocean, not a supercontinent.
wrong.D: The Tethys is a sea.

items.stem: About when did Rodinia assemble?
items.why: Roughly 1.1–0.9 billion years ago, during the Proterozoic.

wrong.A: That is when the Paleozoic ended.
wrong.B: That is the start of the Cambrian.
wrong.D: That is when Earth formed.

items.stem: Rodinia assembled during which eon?
items.why: Assembled during the Proterozoic.

wrong.B: The Hadean is Earth forming its core.
wrong.C: Rodinia came later, about 1.1–0.9 billion years ago.
wrong.D: The Paleozoic is an era that began 539 million years ago.

items.stem: Pangaea was fully assembled during which period?
items.why: Assembled during the Permian Period.

wrong.A: Shallow seas spread over separate continents then.
wrong.C: Pangaea was splitting apart then.
wrong.D: The continents were near their modern positions.

items.stem: Which sequence is correct for Pangaea?
options: Assembled in the Permian, began rifting in the Late Triassic
Assembled in the Triassic, began rifting in the Permian
Assembled in the Cambrian, began rifting in the Ordovician
Assembled in the Jurassic, began rifting in the Cretaceous
items.why: Assembled during the Permian; began rifting apart in the Late Triassic.

wrong.B: The Permian comes before the Triassic.
wrong.C: Far too early.
wrong.D: It was already splitting in the Jurassic.

items.stem: On a paleo-map, the white outlines show...
options: where modern continental regions sit on the ancient map
items.why: From the notes.

wrong.A: The outlines are modern continents.
wrong.C: They show modern regions on the old map.
wrong.D: They outline modern continental regions.

items.stem: Where did the Tethys Sea sit?
options: In the middle of North America
items.why: Must-write: the Tethys Sea sat along its eastern margin.

wrong.A: That was Panthalassa.
wrong.C: Rodinia is a different supercontinent.
wrong.D: The notes place it along Pangaea's eastern margin.

groups.title: Mass Extinction Events
groups.target: I can describe the cause and scale of Earth's two largest mass extinctions in this unit.

items.stem: About when did the end-Permian extinction happen?
items.why: About 252 million years ago, ending the Paleozoic Era.

wrong.A: That is the K–Pg extinction.
wrong.C: That is the start of the Cambrian.
wrong.D: That is the Great Oxidation Event.

items.stem: Which era did the end-Permian extinction end?
items.why: Ending the Paleozoic Era.

wrong.A: The K–Pg ended the Mesozoic.
wrong.B: We are still in the Cenozoic.
wrong.C: The Precambrian ended at the start of the Cambrian.

items.stem: What is the suspected cause of the end-Permian extinction?
items.why: Suspected cause, from the notes.

wrong.A: The most common mix-up: the asteroid is the K–Pg.
wrong.B: Snowball Earth was in the Proterozoic.
wrong.D: Those pace Quaternary ice ages.

items.stem: How did the Siberian Traps change the climate?
options: Blocked sunlight and froze the planet
Released greenhouse gases that drove global warming
Pulled CO₂ out of the air
items.why: Released greenhouse gases directly and by heating carbon-rich rocks, driving global warming.

wrong.A: The end-Permian was warming.
wrong.B: The oceans lost oxygen.
wrong.D: They added greenhouse gases.

items.stem: The Siberian Traps released greenhouse gases directly and also by...
items.why: From the notes.

wrong.A: The notes name carbon-rich rocks.
wrong.B: Coal swamps are Carboniferous.
wrong.C: The oceans warmed and lost oxygen.

items.stem: Which describes the scale of the end-Permian extinction?
options: About 75% of species, including all non-bird dinosaurs
Only a few land species died
items.why: From the notes.

wrong.B: That is the K–Pg.
wrong.C: Land ecosystems suffered severe losses too.
wrong.D: Dinosaurs had not appeared yet.

items.stem: After the end-Permian extinction, how long did it take to rebuild complex ecosystems?
items.why: Rebuilding complex ecosystems took millions of years.

wrong.A: Far too short.
wrong.B: Far too short.
wrong.D: They rebuilt in the Triassic.

items.stem: About when did the K–Pg extinction happen?
items.why: About 66 million years ago, ending the Mesozoic Era.

wrong.D: That is the end-Permian.
wrong.C: That is Archaeopteryx.
wrong.A: That is the end of the Pleistocene.

items.stem: What caused the K–Pg extinction?
options: An asteroid about 10 km wide hit near the Yucatán Peninsula
items.why: A roughly 10 km asteroid struck near today's Yucatán Peninsula (Chicxulub).

wrong.A: That is the end-Permian.
wrong.B: Not the cause named in the notes.
wrong.D: Mammals diversified after the extinction, not before.

items.stem: What is the name of the K–Pg impact crater?
items.why: From the notes.

wrong.B: That is the end-Permian volcanic province.
wrong.C: That is a Cambrian fossil site.
wrong.D: That is the ocean around Pangaea.

items.stem: Which is evidence for the K–Pg impact?
options: A worldwide layer rich in iridium
items.why: An iridium-enriched layer worldwide (also shocked minerals, spherules, tsunami deposits).

wrong.B: Coal is from Carboniferous wetlands.
wrong.C: Those come from glaciers.
wrong.D: That is the end-Permian.

items.stem: About what share of species disappeared in the K–Pg extinction?
items.why: About 75% of species, including all non-avian dinosaurs.

wrong.A: Far too low.
wrong.B: That is the share that survived.
wrong.D: Many survived, including birds and mammals.

items.stem: Which extinction wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs?
items.why: All non-avian dinosaurs disappeared in the K–Pg.

wrong.A: Dinosaurs had not appeared yet.
wrong.B: Far too early.
wrong.D: Far too early.

items.stem: Why do scientists say the dinosaur lineage continues today?
options: Birds are theropod dinosaurs that survived the K–Pg
Some large dinosaurs survived in Antarctica
items.why: Must-write: birds are theropod dinosaurs, and they survived.

wrong.B: All non-bird dinosaurs died.
wrong.C: Pterosaurs are not dinosaurs and did not become birds.
wrong.D: Birds are the surviving dinosaurs.
